props.title: The Ten Commandments

sections.content: Cecil B. DeMille's The Ten Commandments (1956) revolutionized biblical epics with its unprecedented $13 million budget and groundbreaking special effects. Charlton Heston's commanding presence as Moses set the standard for biblical heroes, while the parting of the Red Sea sequence - achieved through innovative practical effects - remains impressive even by today's standards. The film's influence extends to later religious epics like Ben-Hur (1959) and The Greatest Story Ever Told (1965), establishing a visual language for depicting biblical narratives that filmmakers still reference.

sections.content: The cultural impact of The Ten Commandments extends beyond its religious themes. DeMille's masterful use of Technicolor and massive practical sets influenced historical epics for decades, from Cleopatra (1963) to Gladiator (2000). The film's portrayal of ancient Egypt, while historically questionable by modern standards, created an enduring cinematic vocabulary for depicting ancient civilizations that echoes through films like Exodus: Gods and Kings (2014). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Biblical Epics

Modern biblical films have shifted from DeMille's theatrical grandeur to grittier, more naturalistic approaches. The Passion of the Christ (2004) focused on brutal realism, while Noah (2014) and Exodus: Gods and Kings (2014) attempted to merge biblical narrative with contemporary special effects and psychological complexity. Yet none have matched the cultural impact or enduring popularity of The Ten Commandments, which still airs annually on ABC during Easter season.
